questions.q: What is the defining trait of a classic Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) compared to an API gateway?
options: An ESB only handles authentication, never message transformation
An ESB does deep, content-aware work — it looks inside a message, transforms its structure, and routes based on what the message actually contains
An ESB can only be hosted in the cloud, never on-premises
An ESB and an API gateway are simply two names for the identical product
questions.explain: An ESB's defining trait is content-aware processing: it inspects a message's contents, transforms its structure between formats, and can route or orchestrate based on what's actually inside it — work an API gateway generally doesn't do.

questions.q: What question does an API gateway primarily answer, per this lesson?
options: How does this message get translated and routed across several backend transformation steps?
Who is allowed to call this API, how often, and how do I protect the backend from being overwhelmed?
Which programming language should the backend system use?
How should a multi-step business process be orchestrated across five different systems?
questions.explain: An API gateway handles traffic management and policy enforcement at the edge: authentication, rate limiting, logging, and routing to the correct backend version — not content-aware business process orchestration.

questions.q: A mature architecture uses both an API gateway and an iPaaS/ESB layer. What does each one typically handle in that combination?
options: The API gateway does deep content transformation while the iPaaS/ESB handles authentication
The API gateway manages edge traffic and security for incoming calls, while the iPaaS/ESB layer behind it does data transformation and multi-system orchestration
Both layers do exactly the same job, so combining them is redundant
The API gateway is used only for outbound calls, never inbound ones
questions.explain: The two solve different problems: the API gateway sits at the edge managing traffic, authentication, and rate limiting, while the iPaaS/ESB layer behind it performs the actual content-aware transformation and orchestration.

questions.q: Why did classic, monolithic ESBs fall out of favor in modern integration architecture, per this lesson?
options: Because ESBs are illegal under current data-privacy regulations

Because a single heavyweight piece of infrastructure doing routing, transformation, and orchestration all at once becomes a bottleneck, with every integration team depending on the same ESB team and deployment cycle
Because ESBs cannot connect to any cloud-based system such as Salesforce
Because API gateways eliminate the need for any integration layer at all
questions.explain: A monolithic ESB concentrates routing, transformation, and orchestration in one place, making every team that depends on it bottlenecked by the same deployment cycle — the same reason large software monoliths generally fell out of favor.

questions.q: Rate limiting, as described in this lesson, is a concern most associated with which layer?
options: The API gateway, which restricts how many requests a given consumer can make in a time window to protect the backend
The ESB, which uses rate limiting to decide how to transform a message
Neither layer; rate limiting is only a database-level concern
Only the client application calling the API, never the server side
questions.explain: Rate limiting is a traffic-management and policy-enforcement concern handled at the edge by an API gateway, protecting backend systems from being overwhelmed by any single consumer.
